Creatine monohydrate.summary: Widely studied supplement that trials associate with modest gains in strength, lean mass and high-intensity performance.
Creatine monohydrate.overview:
Creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied sports supplement. Creatine itself is a nitrogen-containing compound made in the body from amino acids and also obtained from meat and fish; the monohydrate salt is the standard supplemental form. It is sold as a low-cost, flavourless powder.

In physique and performance circles it is used to support strength, lean mass gain during resistance training and repeated high-intensity effort. Many randomized trials and position stands report modest but consistent gains in these outcomes, and the wiki's evidence rating for it is strong.
Creatine monohydrate.mechanism: Muscle stores creatine mostly as phosphocreatine, which rapidly regenerates ATP during short, intense efforts. Supplementation raises intramuscular creatine content, which researchers say can allow slightly more training work to be done and may encourage greater adaptation over time. Part of the early scale-weight increase is attributed to water drawn into muscle cells.
Creatine monohydrate.risks: Creatine is legal and sold over the counter. Reviews of long-term use in healthy people have found it generally well tolerated, with water retention and occasional gastrointestinal upset the most commonly reported complaints. It can modestly raise serum creatinine without necessarily reflecting kidney damage, which can complicate lab interpretation, and people with kidney disease are advised to seek medical advice first. Responses vary and some people are reported as non-responders.

Whey protein.summary: Fast-digesting milk protein rich in leucine, used to reach daily protein targets and support muscle protein synthesis.
Whey protein.overview:
Whey protein is the liquid fraction of milk left over from cheese making, dried into concentrate, isolate or hydrolysate powders. It is a complete protein that digests quickly and is rich in leucine and other essential amino acids.

Lifters and dieters use it as a convenient way to reach daily protein targets, preserve lean mass while cutting and support muscle gain alongside resistance training. Meta-analyses report a small to moderate benefit for strength and lean mass, larger in older adults and in people who otherwise eat little protein.
Whey protein.mechanism: Whey supplies a rapid rise in blood amino acids, particularly leucine, which stimulates muscle protein synthesis through mTORC1 signalling. Researchers attribute the benefit mainly to adding to total daily protein, so the advantage over other complete protein sources is reported as small when overall intake is already adequate.
Whey protein.risks: Whey is a food product and legal everywhere. Lactose intolerance or milk allergy can cause digestive symptoms or reactions, and isolates contain less lactose. Quality control varies by brand, with occasional heavy-metal or labelling concerns reported. Studies have found no added benefit from very high intakes, and people with kidney disease are advised to follow medical guidance.

Leucine.summary: Essential branched-chain amino acid that activates mTORC1 signalling, the pathway linked to muscle protein synthesis.
Leucine.overview:
Leucine is an essential branched-chain amino acid found in all dietary proteins, with especially high amounts in dairy, meat, eggs and soy. It is also sold as a standalone powder or as part of BCAA and essential amino acid products.

In the muscle-building context it is used to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, particularly in older adults or in people eating little protein. The wiki's strong rating reflects solid mechanistic and acute-response data; research indicates that extra isolated leucine adds little for people who already eat enough complete protein.
Leucine.mechanism: Leucine acts as a signal of amino acid availability. Sensors such as Sestrin2 respond to intracellular leucine and release inhibition of the mTORC1 complex, which promotes translation initiation and muscle protein synthesis. Insulin release triggered by leucine contributes to the same pathway.
Leucine.risks: Leucine is a normal dietary component and legal. High supplemental doses can cause digestive upset and may disturb the balance of other branched-chain amino acids, and leucine is hazardous for people with maple syrup urine disease. Long-term muscle-growth benefits from isolated leucine in healthy, well-fed trainees have not been well demonstrated.

Beta-alanine.summary: Amino acid that raises muscle carnosine and is studied for performance in efforts of one to four minutes; tingling is common.
Beta-alanine.overview:
Beta-alanine is a non-proteinogenic amino acid and the rate-limiting building block of carnosine, a dipeptide stored in skeletal muscle. It is sold as a powder or capsule, often in pre-workout blends.

Athletes use it to improve performance in efforts lasting roughly one to four minutes and to get more work done in high-repetition sets. Studies report a modest effect that does not directly add muscle; the evidence base supports it as an ergogenic aid, and the wiki's rating is strong.
Beta-alanine.mechanism: Taking beta-alanine for several weeks raises muscle carnosine content. Carnosine helps buffer hydrogen ions that accumulate during intense exercise, which is proposed to delay fatigue. The familiar tingling (paraesthesia) comes from activation of sensory nerve receptors and is not considered an indicator of effect.
Beta-alanine.risks: Paraesthesia is the main reported side effect and is described as harmless, though uncomfortable to some; divided or slow-release forms reduce it. Beta-alanine is legal and not banned in sport. Long-term data in healthy adults show no clear toxicity at studied intakes. Studies have found little effect on single-effort maximal strength, with benefits reported mainly for high-rep and endurance-type work.

HMB.summary: Leucine metabolite studied for reducing muscle breakdown, with mixed results that vary by population.
HMB.overview:
HMB (beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate) is a metabolite of leucine, sold as a calcium salt or free acid. It originated in studies of reducing muscle breakdown and has been used by lifters during hard training or calorie restriction.

Results depend heavily on who is studied. Meta-analyses suggest it helps preserve muscle in older adults and in clinical settings, while trials in trained young athletes mostly show little effect; the wiki's rating is moderate.
HMB.mechanism: HMB is thought to reduce protein breakdown through effects on the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and to modestly support protein synthesis signalling and muscle cell repair. Human data for these mechanisms are less consistent than animal and cell work.
HMB.risks: HMB is legal and has a good short-term safety record in trials. Reported side effects are minor, mostly gastrointestinal. Trials in experienced trainees eating enough protein and training progressively have generally not found clear benefits, and product quality is reported to vary.

Citrulline malate.summary: Nitric-oxide precursor used for muscle pump and blood flow; meta-analyses report small, low-certainty performance effects.
Citrulline malate.overview:
Citrulline malate combines the amino acid L-citrulline with malic acid. Citrulline is an intermediate of the urea cycle and a precursor of arginine, and is a common ingredient in pre-workout powders.

It is used for muscle pump, endurance in resistance sets and reduced soreness. Meta-analyses report a small improvement in repetitions to failure with low certainty, and single trials often show no effect.
Citrulline malate.mechanism: Citrulline is converted to arginine in the kidney, which raises nitric oxide production and blood vessel dilation. It may also help clear ammonia and lactate-related fatigue, and malate may feed energy metabolism, though these steps have not been firmly established for performance.
Citrulline malate.risks: Citrulline malate is legal and generally well tolerated; the main reported complaint is stomach upset at larger amounts. It can lower blood pressure slightly, which is relevant for people taking antihypertensive or erectile dysfunction drugs. Benefits for muscle size have not been established.

Betaine.summary: Compound found in beets and shellfish, studied for strength, power and body composition with limited, inconsistent results.
Betaine.overview:
Betaine, also called trimethylglycine, is a small compound found in beets, spinach, wheat and shellfish. It is also produced in the body from choline and sold as a supplement for sports use.

Studies have looked at strength, power and body composition. A meta-analysis suggests a small gain in maximal strength, mainly lower body, while evidence for body composition and power is inconsistent.
Betaine.mechanism: Betaine acts as an osmolyte that protects cells under stress and as a methyl donor, converting homocysteine to methionine. Proposed performance effects include better cell hydration, creatine synthesis support and effects on anabolic signalling, though human data are limited.
Betaine.risks: Betaine is legal and has low acute toxicity. Gastrointestinal upset and a fishy odor can occur, and it may raise cholesterol in some people. It is a prescription medicine for homocystinuria; betaine hydrochloride sold for digestion is a different product. Published trials are small and short.

Ashwagandha.summary: Ayurvedic adaptogen herb; small trials report modest changes in strength, stress and some hormone readings.
Ashwagandha.overview:
Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is a shrub whose root is a staple of Ayurvedic medicine. Extracts are marketed as adaptogens for stress, sleep and vitality.

In fitness use it is taken to support strength, recovery and testosterone. Small randomized trials report modest gains in strength and some hormone readings; the samples are small and funding is often industry-linked, and the wiki's rating is moderate.
Ashwagandha.mechanism: The active constituents are withanolides, which appear to modulate the stress axis, lower cortisol and affect GABAergic and inflammatory signalling. Researchers suggest any effect on muscle likely comes indirectly through improved stress, sleep and recovery rather than direct anabolism.
Ashwagandha.risks: Ashwagandha is sold as a supplement in most countries. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported, and it can affect thyroid hormone levels and cause drowsiness or stomach upset. It is generally avoided in pregnancy and may interact with thyroid, sedative and immunosuppressant drugs.

Turkesterone.summary: Plant ecdysteroid marketed as a natural anabolic; claims rest mainly on rodent data, and small human trials mostly show no clear benefit.
Turkesterone.overview:
Turkesterone is a phytoecdysteroid, a plant steroid structurally related to insect molting hormones, first isolated from Ajuga turkestanica. It became popular in supplements as a purported natural anabolic.

Claims rest largely on rodent studies and on research into the better-known ecdysterone. Human trials of turkesterone specifically are small and mostly have not shown meaningful muscle or strength benefits; the wiki's rating is limited.
Turkesterone.mechanism: In animals, ecdysteroids appear to increase muscle protein synthesis, possibly via estrogen receptor beta and signalling pathways, rather than through the androgen receptor. How well turkesterone is absorbed and whether these findings apply to people are unresolved.
Turkesterone.risks: It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, with unresolved novel-food status in the EU. Short-term human studies have not reported serious harm, but long-term data are lacking, and independent testing has found products containing far less turkesterone than labelled.

Ecdysterone.summary: Plant and insect steroid with one widely cited study reporting greater muscle gains in young men; evidence is preliminary.
Ecdysterone.overview:
Ecdysterone, or 20-hydroxyecdysone, is the main molting hormone of insects and crustaceans and is also found in plants such as spinach and Cyanotis. It is sold as a supplement and is being developed as an investigational drug for some muscle conditions.

A widely cited study in young men reported greater muscle gains with high-dose ecdysterone alongside training; replication is lacking and other findings are mixed, so the evidence is considered preliminary.
Ecdysterone.mechanism: In rodents ecdysterone stimulates muscle protein synthesis without androgen receptor activity, with evidence pointing to estrogen receptor beta and downstream Akt signalling. Human mechanism data are limited.
Ecdysterone.risks: Acute toxicity appears low. It is sold as a supplement, but the World Anti-Doping Agency has monitored it, and product purity is reported to be variable. Long-term human safety has not been established.

Testosterone.summary: Principal male androgen; prescribed for diagnosed hypogonadism and also used non-medically for muscle, bone density and secondary sex characteristics.
Testosterone.note: Evidence of benefit is strong in diagnosed deficiency; serious risks are documented with use outside indicated treatment.
Testosterone.overview:
Testosterone is the principal male sex hormone, an androgen produced mainly in the testes. It drives male secondary sexual characteristics, bone density, red blood cell production and muscle mass.

In medicine it is prescribed to treat diagnosed hypogonadism. Healthy young men given supraphysiologic doses gain muscle in a dose-dependent way, and anabolic steroid use is a feature of physique culture. Evidence of benefit is strong where there is true deficiency; use beyond that is associated with serious documented risks.
Testosterone.mechanism: Testosterone binds the androgen receptor, increasing muscle protein synthesis, satellite cell activity and bone formation, and is partly converted to estradiol and dihydrotestosterone, which have their own effects.
Testosterone.risks: It is a prescription-only, controlled substance in many countries. Documented risks include suppression of natural production and fertility, acne, polycythemia, blood pressure and lipid changes, mood effects and possible cardiovascular strain; abrupt cessation can leave a deficiency. This entry is informational and not guidance for use.

Somatropin.summary: Recombinant human growth hormone; acts through IGF-1 signalling and alters body composition, with documented side effects.
Somatropin.note: Evidence is strong for deficiency; chronic excess is documented to enlarge facial features as a disease process (acromegaly).
Somatropin.overview:
Somatropin is recombinant human growth hormone, identical in sequence to the pituitary hormone. It is a prescription medicine for children and adults with growth hormone deficiency and several other conditions.

It is also used illicitly for body composition and anti-aging. Evidence is strong in deficiency; in healthy people studies report it can add some lean mass, with limited strength benefit and notable side effects.
Somatropin.mechanism: It binds growth hormone receptors and activates JAK2/STAT signalling, which prompts the liver and other tissues to produce IGF-1. The result is growth, fat mobilization and effects on glucose metabolism and fluid balance.
Somatropin.risks: Somatropin is prescription-only and banned in sport. Side effects include fluid retention, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and insulin resistance. Chronic excess causes acromegaly, with enlargement of the jaw, brow and hands, plus heart and metabolic problems and a possible cancer link. This is informational, not guidance for use.

MK-677.summary: Oral ghrelin agonist that raises GH, IGF-1 and appetite; no aesthetic benefit has been demonstrated in trials.
MK-677.overview:
MK-677 (ibutamoren) is an orally active, non-peptide drug that mimics ghrelin and raises growth hormone and IGF-1. It was developed by Merck but never approved, and is sold as a research chemical.

Trials in older adults and obese men showed increased fat-free mass but no clear functional improvement, and no cosmetic benefit has been demonstrated; the wiki's rating is unproven.
MK-677.mechanism: It activates the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a) in the pituitary and hypothalamus, producing pulsatile growth hormone release and downstream IGF-1 elevation, plus increased appetite.
MK-677.risks: Not approved for any use and prohibited in sport. Reported effects include increased appetite, fluid retention, lethargy and reduced insulin sensitivity; a heart failure signal appeared in one trial. Long-term effects of sustained IGF-1 elevation are unknown, and products may be mislabelled.

CJC-1295.summary: Synthetic GHRH analogue that raises growth hormone release; human endocrine data are limited and no muscle or cosmetic benefit has been shown.
CJC-1295.overview:
CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone developed in the early 2000s. The long-acting version binds albumin, extending its half-life.

Early human studies showed raised growth hormone and IGF-1, but development stopped and no data show a muscle or cosmetic benefit; the wiki's rating is unproven.
CJC-1295.mechanism: It binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotrophs, increasing growth hormone secretion and IGF-1 levels for days after a single administration in the long-acting form.
CJC-1295.risks: It is not an approved medicine, is sold as a research peptide, and is banned in sport. A phase II trial was halted after a death in a participant. Reported effects include flushing, headache, water retention and injection-site reactions. Long-term safety is unknown and the regulatory status of compounded versions has been in flux.

Ipamorelin.summary: Selective growth hormone secretagogue sold as a research peptide; human data are sparse.
Ipamorelin.overview:
Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide that selectively stimulates growth hormone release. Novo Nordisk developed it in the 1990s, and it is now sold as a research peptide.

Clinical work has been limited, mainly early pharmacology and a trial in post-surgical bowel recovery that showed no clear benefit. Good human data supporting claims for muscle and fat loss have not been published.
Ipamorelin.mechanism: It is a selective agonist of the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a), triggering pulsatile pituitary growth hormone release with relatively little effect on cortisol and prolactin compared with older secretagogues.
Ipamorelin.risks: It is not approved for human use and is banned in sport. Short-term data are limited; theoretical concerns include insulin resistance, fluid retention and effects of long-term GH/IGF-1 elevation. Product quality is unregulated.

Sermorelin.summary: GHRH analogue that stimulates natural growth hormone release; its hormonal effect is documented, but cosmetic benefit is unproven.
Sermorelin.overview:
Sermorelin is a synthetic fragment of growth hormone releasing hormone consisting of its first 29 amino acids. It was FDA-approved for diagnosing and treating growth hormone deficiency in children before manufacturing ceased in 2008.

It is still available through compounding pharmacies and used off-label for age-related decline. Its hormonal mechanism is documented, while evidence for visible body-composition or cosmetic benefit is limited.
Sermorelin.mechanism: It acts on GHRH receptors in the pituitary to prompt natural, pulsatile growth hormone release, so the body's feedback mechanisms still operate, unlike with injected GH.
Sermorelin.risks: It is prescription-only in the US and banned in competitive sport. Common effects are injection-site reactions, flushing and headache. It is avoided with active cancer and in pregnancy. Quality of compounded preparations and the claims made in telehealth marketing are reported to vary.

GHRP-6.summary: First-generation GH-releasing peptide sold as a research chemical; known for raising growth hormone and strongly increasing hunger.
GHRP-6.overview:
GHRP-6 is a synthetic hexapeptide from the first generation of growth hormone releasing peptides. It was a research tool in the 1980s and 1990s and is now sold as a research chemical.

It is known for raising growth hormone and also for a strong hunger effect. Human evidence of improved muscle or appearance has not been published.
GHRP-6.mechanism: GHRP-6 activates the ghrelin receptor, causing growth hormone release and appetite stimulation, and also raises cortisol and prolactin somewhat.
GHRP-6.risks: It is not approved for human use and is banned in sport. Reported effects include intense hunger, water retention and flushing. Long-term safety is unknown and quality is unregulated.

IGF-1 LR3.summary: Modified IGF-1 analogue sold to bodybuilders as a research chemical; no reliable human trials of benefit exist.
IGF-1 LR3.overview:
IGF-1 LR3 is a lab-modified version of insulin-like growth factor 1 with an extended amino acid chain and an arginine substitution. It was developed for cell culture and sold to bodybuilders as an injectable research chemical.

Animal and cell data show growth effects, but no reliable human trials of benefit in healthy people have been published.
IGF-1 LR3.mechanism: It activates the IGF-1 receptor and downstream PI3K/Akt/mTOR signalling. The modifications lower binding to IGF binding proteins, so it stays active longer than native IGF-1.
IGF-1 LR3.risks: Not approved for humans and banned in sport. Main concerns are low blood sugar, fluid retention, joint pain and organ growth, plus theoretical cancer promotion. Products are unregulated.

Follistatin-344.summary: Peptide sold as an experimental myostatin blocker; human evidence exists for gene therapy but not for injected peptide products.
Follistatin-344.overview:
Follistatin-344 refers to a form of the protein follistatin (the 344 label is used by peptide vendors) sold as an experimental myostatin blocker. Follistatin is a natural protein that binds and neutralizes myostatin and activins.

Gene therapy work in animals and early clinical trials shows muscle effects, but no credible human evidence exists for injected peptide products.
Follistatin-344.mechanism: Follistatin binds myostatin and activin, preventing them from signalling through their receptors, which relieves the brake on muscle growth in animal models.
Follistatin-344.risks: Not approved; banned in sport. Because follistatin affects reproductive hormones and other tissues, blocking these pathways raises theoretical concerns. Marketed peptides are unregulated and may not contain what is claimed.

Ostarine.summary: Most-studied SARM, developed for muscle wasting and never approved; trials show lean mass gains and it suppresses natural testosterone.
Ostarine.overview:
Ostarine (enobosarm, MK-2866) is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator developed to treat muscle wasting. It reached phase III trials but was never approved.

Trials showed lean mass gains without matching functional gains. Recreational use is common and a frequent cause of anti-doping violations.
Ostarine.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor, aiming for activity in muscle and bone with less effect on tissues such as the prostate. It suppresses natural testosterone production.
Ostarine.risks: Not approved and banned in sport. Reported harms include hormonal suppression, lipid changes and drug-induced liver injury. Gray-market products are often mislabelled.

LGD-4033.summary: SARM investigated for muscle wasting; small trials report lean mass gains, alongside hormonal suppression and lipid changes.
LGD-4033.overview:
LGD-4033 (ligandrol) is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator investigated for muscle wasting. A phase I study found increased lean mass in healthy men, but development stalled.

It is widely sold as a research chemical. Small trials show lean mass gains, and observations of recreational use report hormone and lipid problems.
LGD-4033.mechanism: It selectively activates the androgen receptor in muscle and bone and suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, lowering natural testosterone.
LGD-4033.risks: Not approved and banned in sport. Documented problems include testosterone suppression, reduced HDL cholesterol and drug-induced liver injury, especially at doses above trial levels. Product contents are unreliable.

RAD-140.summary: Potent investigational SARM with little human data; case reports link it to liver injury and it suppresses hormones.
RAD-140.overview:
RAD-140 (testolone) is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator developed by Radius Health, studied in preclinical models for muscle and breast cancer. It has never completed human efficacy trials.

It is sold as a research chemical for muscle gain, with little human data.
RAD-140.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor with tissue selectivity and suppresses natural androgen production.
RAD-140.risks: Not approved and banned in sport. Case reports link it to drug-induced liver injury, and it suppresses hormones. Evidence of its safety is insufficient. Products may be mislabelled.

YK-11.summary: Experimental steroid-based compound classed as a SARM; research is limited to cell studies and no human trials exist.
YK-11.overview:
YK-11 is an experimental steroid-based compound classed as a SARM, though it behaves as a partial androgen receptor agonist. Research is confined to cell studies, mainly from Japanese groups in 2011 to 2013.

It is sold as a research chemical. No human trials exist.
YK-11.mechanism: In cultured muscle cells it increased follistatin expression and reduced myostatin signalling via androgen receptor activation. These results have not been shown in humans.
YK-11.risks: Not approved and banned in sport. Safety is untested in humans, and liver, hormonal and cardiovascular effects are suspected. Products sold online are frequently mislabelled.
